title.narrative: Increasing Integrated Health Resilience in Yemen (IHRP I)

description.narrative: Continuing and extending Yamaan's efforts and build on its capacity and expertise in the different governorates; this is to increase the uptake of quality SMH and contraceptive services, leading to improved RHR of Yemeni women in the target governorates and strengthen the capacity of health facilities in these locations through the VMP. The VMP with integrated health resilience will include the following areas of intervention:•Demand-side: By targeting the vulnerable and high-risk populations mainly through implementing the voucher scheme for safe motherhood (SMH) and FP, in addition to allocating some funds for the provision of medications to people suffering from chronic NCDs. Limited provision will be made in the budget to provide more direct crisis support for NCDs. It is a crucial priority for the health facilities Yamaan work in and will improve the services. The most vulnerable people suffering from NCDs within the catchment area of the health facilities will be targeted based on the facility data and discussion with local authorities and joint prioritization.•Supply-side: By implementing the voucher scheme together with the performance-based financing (PBF) component in addition to refurbishing and providing essential equipment to public health facilities. Yamaan aims to ensure operational support to the public health facilities through performance-based financial support and reimbursements. It will also ensure that some public health facilities in the target districts that Yamaan cannot include in the voucher scheme due to not meeting the minimum requirements could be supported under this area to improve and eventually meet the minimum requirements, eventually joining the voucher scheme. Strengthening the public health facilities that are part of the program by integrating the (PBF) mechanism to provide additional incentives for providers to strengthen the health system in their locations. By injecting additional income through these facilities (supply-side financing mechanism), they will be supported to provide services more sustainably and make some much-needed transformation to infrastructure that has been weakened by the long-lasting conflict and further weakened due to multiple epidemics. PBF is an additional form of financing, on top of traditional public financing, that provides financial rewards to service providers for delivering agreed outputs upon verifying that the agreed-upon and reported performance had taken place.Integrating this component in the same target areas will improve the infrastructure and access to some health facilities, especially those excluded by the quality assessment of the voucher and PBF due to a lack of sufficient infrastructure requirements. These facilities could then be included in the voucher or PBF for continuous improvements and quality of services.•Preparedness and response to epidemics: By supporting the health sector's preparedness and readiness to multi-dimensional health risks like epidemics, including COVID-19, which overburden the already weak health system and affect its overall capacity both on supply and demand sides. This component of the program will play a crucial role in preventing, detecting, and responding to epidemic-prone diseases such as COVID-19, cholera, and vector-borne diseases such as dengue fever and malaria and other prevalent communicable diseases in Yemen, including through support to rapid response teams and pre-positioning outbreak supplies.By such an approach, Yamaan takes into consideration the national health priorities published by authorities as well as the Heath Cluster priority response, which is centered around three objectives: 1.To strengthen preparedness and surveillance, including early detection and response measures to communicable diseases, outbreaks, and epidemics like COVID-19.2.To increase access of vulnerable populations, including internally displaced people (IDPs), to the Minimum Health Service Package, supporting the health system and community resilience at all levels, and prioritizing RH, mental health and psychosocial support, severe malnutrition response and management of NCDs; and 3.To strengthen the health system and operational support to health facilities, including through fuel, water, oxygen, health information management, financial support to healthcare workers and the provision of essential support to critically needed advanced care (such as renal dialysis centers, cancer care facilities and intensive care units) in priority districts.

recipient-country.narrative: system is struggling to cope under the pressure of the continuing emergency. More than half of all health facilities are closed due to damage, destruction, or lack of funds. The largest cholera epidemic in the world is currently spreading across Yemen, exacerbated by deteriorating hygiene and sanitation conditions and disruptions to the water supply. 84 percent of Yemen’s estimated 2.9 million internally displaced persons have been displaced for over a year, resulting in additional needs due to depleted savings, lack of access to financial resources and the saturation of available housing capacity. Despite a decline since 1990, maternal mortality ratio (MMR) in Yemen remains among the highest in the region, at 385 deaths per 100,000 live births. The risk is significantly higher for marginalized and vulnerable groups: the MMR in rural areas is 69 percent higher than urban areas, and 80 percent of maternal deaths are among women and girls with less than primary education. The intervening two and a half years of conflict have worsened the situation considerably since these statistics were captured. Women and girls have fewer of the protective factors commonly available to men and boys to mitigate the impact of crisis and emergency: income, assets, access to health and education, social networks, political voice, legal protection and the realization of basic human rights. The incidence of gender-based violence also increases during conflict, with early/forced marriage becoming more common. These factors increase the likelihood of unintended pregnancy and the associated risk. Contraception and safe motherhood services are particularly important under these conditions to enable women to delay and space pregnancies and access vital medical assistance before, during and after childbirth. In 2013, only 45 percent of births were attended by skilled health staff and only 30 percent were in a health facility. 62 percent of women had a need for contraception but only 27 percent were using it. Given the deteriorating health facilities, lack of service providers and essential supplies, it is an even greater challenge for women to access services today. Many women and girls, particularly in rural areas, lack the funds to pay for transport and service costs associated with accessing the formal health system.
